# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) are a cornerstone therapy for the prevention of sudden cardiac death in both primary and secondary prevention populations [1]. For decades, transvenous ICDs (TV-ICDs) were the standard of care, yet they carry a well-recognized burden of lead-related complications. For decades, conventional transvenous ICDs were the standard of care, but these devices are associated with a risk of complications related to transvenous leads, such as infection, pneumothorax, and lead dysfunction. The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was conceived to circumvent these intravascular hazards. The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter–defibrillator was designed to avoid complications related to the transvenous ICD lead by using an entirely extrathoracic placement.

## Development and Early Evidence

The proof-of-concept for an entirely extrathoracic system was established in a landmark study by Bardy and colleagues. Bardy and colleagues tested four different subcutaneous ICD configurations in 78 patients, ultimately settling on a parasternal electrode and a left lateral thoracic pulse generator configuration, then tested that configuration in 49 patients and established that the device was as capable as a traditional transvenous device of achieving defibrillation, though the subcutaneous device required a greater energy expenditure. [2] These findings were extended by an early single-center chronic validation experience [3] and by the pivotal Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) study, which demonstrated the safety and efficacy of a totally subcutaneous device [4].

Real-world performance was characterized by the EFFORTLESS registry [5,6]. In its long-term analysis, first and final shock efficacy for discrete ventricular arrhythmias was consistent at 90% and 98%, respectively, with storm episode final shock efficacy at 95.2%. Notably, of the explants, only 2.0% of patients needed a transvenous device for pacing indications [6]. A pooled two-year analysis of the IDE study and EFFORTLESS registry further confirmed acceptable safety and efficacy [7].

## Randomized Comparisons with the Transvenous ICD

The PRAETORIAN trial provided the first randomized head-to-head comparison [8]. PRAETORIAN was an international, multicentre, randomized trial in which 849 patients with an indication for ICD therapy were randomized to receive an S-ICD or TV-ICD and followed for a median of 49 months [9]. It showed noninferiority of the S-ICD with regard to the composite end point of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks after 49.1 months [10]. A prespecified secondary analysis examined the full complication profile across both arms [11], and because lead-related complications accrue over longer periods, the PRAETORIAN-XL trial is now evaluating whether the S-ICD is superior at 8-year follow-up [10].

The ATLAS trial enrolled a younger, higher-risk population [12]. A composite of lead-related complications had occurred in one patient who received an S-ICD and 12 who received a transvenous ICD by 6 months, a 92% relative reduction with the S-ICD [13]. A randomized comparison within ATLAS also showed that patients with an S-ICD were seven times less likely to experience worsening tricuspid regurgitation compared to those with a TV-ICD [14]. The UNTOUCHED study evaluated the device specifically in primary-prevention patients with low ejection fraction [15].

Pooled syntheses corroborate these signals. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized and propensity-matched studies confirmed reduced lead-related complications with the S-ICD, while all-cause mortality was not significantly different between modalities [16,17].

## Inappropriate Shocks and Patient Selection

The principal trade-off of the S-ICD is a propensity for inappropriate shocks driven by oversensing. In an individual-participant meta-analysis of randomized trials, a first inappropriate shock occurred more frequently in patients randomized to subcutaneous compared with transvenous ICDs (2.5 vs 1.5 per 100 patient-years) [18]. The mechanisms differ by device: patients with subcutaneous ICDs had a higher hazard of inappropriate shock due to cardiac oversensing and electromagnetic interference or myopotentials but a lower hazard due to atrial arrhythmia [18]. In the EFFORTLESS registry, 48 out of 581 patients experienced inappropriate shocks (8.3%), the most common cause being cardiac signal oversensing such as T-wave oversensing [19].

Because detection is based on the surface electrogram, preimplant electrocardiographic screening is essential. In one cohort, eight percent of potential S-ICD patients were not eligible after failing the screening test designed to identify patients susceptible to T-wave oversensing [20]. Refinements such as dual-zone programming, the SMART Pass filter, and lessons from MADIT-RIT on prolonged detection and high-rate cutoffs have substantially reduced inappropriate therapy [21,22]. Newer sensing algorithms have further lowered these rates [23], and air entrapment has been recognized as a transient early cause of oversensing [24].

The PRAETORIAN score, derived from chest radiographs, estimates defibrillation success based on device and lead positioning [25], and the PRAETORIAN-DFT trial is assessing whether routine defibrillation testing can be safely omitted [26].

## Limitations and Future Directions

The chief limitation of the S-ICD is the absence of bradycardia pacing, antitachycardia pacing (ATP), and cardiac resynchronization. Because of the lack of endocardial pacing components, patients with long-term pacing needs are ineligible for the S-ICD [27]. Two technological advances address this gap. The MODULAR ATP trial paired the S-ICD with a wirelessly communicating leadless pacemaker; the percentage of arrhythmia episodes successfully terminated by antitachycardia pacing was 61.3%, with no failures due to device miscommunication [28]. Separately, the extravascular ICD (EV ICD) places a substernal lead. Substernal lead placement permits both defibrillation at thresholds similar to those seen with transvenous ICDs and effective anti-tachycardia pacing while avoiding the vasculature [29].

## Conclusion

The S-ICD has matured into an established alternative to the TV-ICD, offering a clear reduction in lead-related complications without compromising defibrillation efficacy or survival, at the cost of a modest excess of inappropriate shocks and a lack of pacing capability. Contemporary guidelines endorse its use in appropriately selected patients [30], and emerging modular and extravascular technologies promise to extend extravascular therapy to patients who require pacing.
